text: Humans remember names; computers route by number. DNS is the lookup service that turns a name like www.example.com into the IP address a router can actually forward traffic to. Resolving that name isn't one lookup — it's a chain of them, and that chain is exactly what makes DNS troubleshooting make sense once you've seen it laid out.

Your laptop asks its recursive resolver, which does all the work on your behalf. If it doesn't already have the answer cached, it asks a root server who handles dot-com, gets pointed to the dot-com TLD server, and that server points it to the authoritative server for example dot com — the one place that actually holds the real record.

Real record types show up constantly: A maps a name to an IPv4 address, AAAA to IPv6, CNAME is an alias pointing to another name, MX lists which mail server handles the domain's email, TXT holds free-form text like SPF and DKIM verification, and NS lists which servers are authoritative for the domain.

nslookup and dig both query DNS directly. nslookup's Non-authoritative answer simply means the reply came from the resolver's cache, not fresh from the domain's own server. dig's answer section shows the record plus its remaining TTL in seconds — proof of exactly how much longer that cached answer is still considered valid.

Every record publishes a TTL — how long a resolver may cache it before asking again. A low TTL means changes propagate fast, at the cost of more queries hitting the authoritative server. A high TTL means less load, but a change made today might not reach everyone around the world for up to a full day afterward.

That's exactly why anyone planning a real DNS cutover lowers the TTL days in advance. Next up, Lesson 8 covers DHCP — how a device gets a full IP configuration automatically, the instant it joins a network, with no human involved at all.
